title: Inference win-wires — enterprise sales messaging & objection registry
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact set of "win-wires" for AE/SEs to use when positioning Redwood Inference against LLM API providers (both hosted and managed endpoint competitors). Focus is on concise rebuttals, escalation points, and demo triggers — optimized for mid-to-late stage enterprise procurement conversations where latency, predictability, and compliance are the levers.

Audience:
- Account Executives and Solutions Engineers
- Sales leadership prepping for RFP reviews
- Customer success managers during onboarding

High-level positioning pillars (one-liners to memorize):
1) Predictable economics for production: we design for per-request unit economics (batching, cache, routing) so customers see stable cost per 1M tokens across traffic patterns.
2) Same API, multiple deployment profiles: Hosted API -> Dedicated pools -> Private VPC/air-gapped option with the same operational controls and rollouts.
3) Production-first reliability & graceful degradation: built-in fallback routing, variant rollouts, and SLA-backed Dedicated capacity.
4) Observability tied to quality: token-level cost + per-route evals & regression alerts (so teams can spot silent quality regressions in model rollouts).

Competitor shorthand (how prospects typically frame them):
- Big Cloud Managed APIs (Provider A): "easy, integrated with cloud infra" — wins on familiarity; weak where customers need strict inference economics and deterministic latency.
- LLM API challengers (Provider B/C): "fast iteration + lower sticker" — can be good for prototypes but slip on enterprise telemetry, model governance, and private deployments.
- Self-hosted runtimes (OSS + infra): "full control" — attractive on paper but high ops burden (cost, headcount, long tail bugs).

Quick feature comparison bullets (talk tracks + one-liner rebuttals):
- Deterministic throughput & latency SLAs: Redwood offers Dedicated pools with latency SLOs and predictable autoscale; rebuttal: "turnkey SLAs + committed capacity = no surprises at peak".
- Cost controls (per-route token breakdowns, batching/caching suggestions): Redwood shows token-level cost drivers and prescriptive Optimize recommendations; rebuttal: "We give teams levers, not black boxes." 
- Private deployment and VPC parity: Redwood Private supports the same rollout and observability features as Hosted; rebuttal: "You don't trade features for security." 
- Model fallback & routing policies: automatic fallback to cheaper/compatible variants with health checks; rebuttal: "If the primary model has an outage, your product keeps serving." 
- Eval-driven quality monitoring: regression alerts tied to labeled prompt sets; rebuttal: "We detect silent drift before it reaches customers." 

Common objections and suggested playbook responses (short + tactical):
1) "We can just use the major cloud's managed model endpoints to reduce complexity."
  - Response: "Managed endpoints are great for APIs, but many teams discover variability in tail latency and token costs when they scale. We provide Dedicated capacity and per-token telemetry to avoid those surprises — here's a case study (link)."
  - Demo trigger: show token-level cost heatmap for a mixed workload (conversational + embedding bursts).

2) "We prefer open-source self-hosted to avoid vendor lock-in and cost."
  - Response: "Self-hosting gives control but shifts the entire ops burden (GPU tuning, kernel selection, batching heuristics). Redwood's runtime encodes those optimizations and we offer Private installs when lock-in is a legal concern — plus an escape hatch: exportable model artifacts and documented configs."
  - Escalation: Introduce Solution Architect and share an on-prem pilot plan (JIRA-INF-342).

3) "Your pricing looks higher for steady-state throughput vs spot cloud GPUs."
  - Response: "Spot GPUs can look cheaper but unpredictability leads to higher effective costs: pause/retry logic, extended latencies, and higher engineering churn. Our Optimize toolkit specifically models total cost of ownership and shows where batching/caching recovers unit economics."
  - Demo trigger: run the TCO workbook live with prospect's traffic sample.

4) "We need SOC2 / ISO / KMS integration — can you satisfy compliance?"
  - Response: "Yes. Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and we have an enterprise compliance package; for Hosted we provide audit logs and SOC2 attestation. We'll loop in security to do a tech due-diligence call."

5) "What happens if you go down or have a model regression?"
  - Response: "We have multi-tier graceful degradation: model variant fallbacks, region failover, and automatic circuit-breakers. For regressions, our eval alerts map directly to prompt sets and we can auto-fallback to a conservative policy while the model is rolled back."

Subtle traps to use in demos / qualification (not rhetorical — concrete checks):
- Ask about tail-latency SLAs and how they currently measure 99th percentile during load spikes. If they can't show measurement, push a short benchmark (we offer a sandbox script).
- Probe for hidden costs: re-runs, retries, multiple fine-tuned variants per tenant. Show how per-route token accounting surfaces that leakage.
- When they praise "single-provider convenience," ask about cross-region traffic and compliance constraints — open the door to Dedicated/Private conversation.

Demo checklist (what to have ready for an AE/SE demo focused on economics + reliability):
- 2-minute architecture slide: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (visuals we can reuse)
- Live token-cost heatmap for a sample app (conversational + batch embedding)
- Canary rollout demo: how to push a model change and observe eval/regression alert, then rollback
- Failure injection: region fallback + variant routing in action
- Quick TCO calc with prospect inputs (sheet link)

RFP/RFI language snippets (copy-paste friendly):
- "Redwood Inference provides a unified API across hosted, dedicated and private deployments, with SLA-backed Dedicated capacity, token-level billing and first-class observability for model quality and cost. Dedicated and Private deployments support KMS/HSM and audit logging for regulated workloads."

On pricing asks and negotiation levers:
- Commitments buy latency/capacity guarantees. Use reserved capacity to lock predictable throughput at a discount.
- Offer a 60–90 day pilot with capped ingress, include a one-time optimization review (runtime tuning + batching suggestions) as technical onboarding value.
- For procurement, package the compliance add-on rather than discounting list price: creates perceived value and preserves ARR.

Open questions / TODOs (work-in-progress content — action items for the GTM squad):
- [ ] Assemble 2–3 short customer stories quantifying cost savings after Optimize recommendations (owner: Elena).
- [ ] Build a one-click benchmark runner for AEs to share with prospects (owner: DevTools, ticket: GH #21).
- [ ] Update the sales demo script to include the failure-injection scenario (owner: Samir).
- [ ] Create a one-pager comparing private install checklist vs typical self-host runbook (owner: Ravi).

Slack channels / rapid-contacts when prospect escalates security or infra questions:
- #sales-security (internal) — for compliance escalations
- #se-oncall — for immediate demo help (callout: pager for region-failover demo)
- Solutions Architect on-call roster: Samir D., Elena G.

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep examples concrete and metric-focused — engineering buyers care about p99, tail cost, and dev hours saved.
- Avoid generic "we're faster" claims without numbers. Use 95/99 latency comparisons and batch-cold-vs-warm KV cache examples.
- This doc should be a living artifact — mark sections where we need concrete customer metrics.

Bottom line for reps:
Lead with predictable economics + deployment parity. Use Dedicated/Private as the answer for reliability/compliance objections. Convert pricing pushbacks into pilots that surface real TCO benefits via Optimize recommendations.
